artifacts.notes: Keyed text, not OCR. guidance/catena.md recorded that the unencumbered Latin is OCR wreckage and the clean Latin encumbered, measuring Migne PL 34's Internet Archive text layer at roughly one corrupted word in eight; that is true of the scan and false of the volume. This is the University of Zurich's Corpus Corporum encoding of Migne PL 91, keyed rather than scanned, republished on Latin Wikisource under a stated CC BY-SA 4.0 markup licence over a public-domain printing. It is a transcription of a web witness of that printing and not a collation against the printed column, so no passage taken from it rises above inspected.

artifacts.notes: The work occupies one wiki page and that page is the whole of it: the letter to Acca and all four books, current revision 267515 at retrieval. The page carries the Corpus Corporum encoding note recording that the file was encoded in TEI XML for the University of Zurich's Corpus Corporum project from Migne's Patrologia Latina tomus 91; that is the encoder's statement about the file and is not part of Migne, and the transformation removes it.
artifacts.rights_basis: Bede's Latin is of the eighth century and Migne's printing is of 1850, so the text beneath these bytes is in the public domain everywhere. The bytes themselves are the wiki source of a Latin Wikisource transcription, and Latin Wikisource contributions are licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 — a condition on the contributors' markup rather than on Migne's text under it. The exact bytes are therefore hashed and recorded but not retained here, and only the printed Latin reaches the tracked derivative, stripped of every template, link, heading and column marker the contributors and the encoder added.

edition.notes: Migne prints the work in four books under the title Hexaemeron, preceded by Bede's letter to Acca. The printing marks no chapter and no verse anywhere: every paragraph simply opens with the Vulgate lemma it is about, which is what bounds each fragment here. No public-domain English translation exists: C. B. Kendall's, Translated Texts for Historians 48, 2008, is the first and is in copyright, so the work is held in Latin only and the site says so.

work.author: Bede
work.description: Bede's commentary on the opening of Genesis, in four books, running from the first verse to the expulsion of Ishmael at Genesis 21:10 and no further. Its preface to Acca of Hexham states the method plainly: what Basil, Ambrose and Augustine wrote on these chapters is too long and too deep for ordinary readers, so Bede gathers from them what an unlearned reader can use, sometimes in their words and sometimes in his own. Migne titles it Hexaemeron, which names only the first of its four books.
work.title: In principium Genesis
